whatTheyArgued: Nothing: the Nights is an anonymous medieval story collection, not an argument. Scheherazade is a character, not an author. In the frame story (Burton 1885, vol. I, snipped) she tells her sister that she will tell a tale as their deliverance, to turn the King from his blood-thirsty custom. Within her tales characters tell further tales, so the work has layered nesting. Nothing in the text states a rule that each 'I' is bound to its declaring frame; that is a narratological reading (our own, or Genette-style) laid over the work.

scholarship.ref: Wikipedia, One Thousand and One Nights (frame story, nested narratives, textual history); a general reference, not peer-reviewed. I found no SEP/IEP entry on the Nights.
scholarship.supports: frame narrative; a character in a tale may tell a tale of their own, which may nest another
scholarship.disputes: No single canonical text: Syrian vs Egyptian traditions; Mahdi's Leiden edition is the only critical edition; Galland added tales (Aladdin) absent from Arabic manuscripts; Burton is one of several translations, itself disputed for emphasis

ourUse: speaker.js reads the declared headings of epistolary sections (journal, diary, letter) and binds each 'I' to that section's declared author via a binding table. The Dracula-style document heading is the whole mechanism. The header says it follows the nested tales of the Nights 'however deep the nesting goes', but grep of speaker.js finds no nesting-depth handling, only the Handle line mentions nesting.

bends.ours: speaker.js opens with a block headed 'Scheherazade speaks:' quoting the Burton passage, then a paragraph saying the file 'is the embodiment of Scheherazade's skill' and 'My teaching demands that this file remain a testament to the art of storytelling'. That paragraph is generated text in Scheherazade's first person.
bends.theirs: The Nights contains no such statement; Scheherazade never says anything about speaker boundaries or this file. Only the snipped Burton sentence is hers.

bends.ours: The snip (her plan to tell a tale as deliverance) is offered as the teaching behind 'each I bound to its frame'.
bends.theirs: The snipped sentence is the frame-story premise; it says nothing about frames, narrators or binding of 'I'. It is a thematic epigraph, not support.

bends.ours: Handle line and compendium: nested tellers 'however deep the nesting goes'.
bends.theirs: The Nights does nest tellers, but our code implements one level: epistolary section headings in a modern novel, a different structure from oral tale nesting marked by narration verbs, and it has no depth stack.

bends.ours: Compendium work: 'the tale-within-the-tale's narrator is never the outer narrator'.
bends.theirs: A narratological principle, not stated in the Nights; in the Nights the outer narrator reports all inner tellers, and Scheherazade herself is framed by an anonymous voice.

fix: compendium work: 'The frame-story heroine of the Nights, whose tales nest further tellers (Burton 1885 vol. I). We borrow the image only: speaker.js binds each epistolary "I" to its section's declared author; it does not model oral tale nesting.'
